q: A dog presented under suspicion of sexual abuse has a normal physical examination with no external injuries. Which statement BEST reflects how to proceed?
o: Only proceed with the workup if law enforcement confirms sexual abuse occurred
Proceed with bathing the animal first to allow a cleaner examination
Absence of injury does not exclude sexual abuse — proceed with the full 9-step forensic protocol including ALS examination, DNA swabs, and cavity flush
The absence of injuries excludes sexual abuse — no further workup is needed
e: "No injuries does NOT exclude" is the core principle of sexual abuse forensic examination. Many animals show no gross injuries. Microscopic findings (spermatozoa on cytology or UA), DNA evidence on swabs, and ALS-detectable biological fluids may be present even when the physical exam is entirely normal. Always proceed with the full protocol. Do not bathe before forensic evidence collection, and do not wait for confirmation from law enforcement — the examination IS the investigative step.

q: During the ASPCA sexual abuse forensic protocol, rectal temperature should be taken at which step?
o: Last — after all rectal swabs, flush samples, and physical examination are complete
After ALS examination but before swab collection
First, as part of baseline vital sign assessment before any other procedures
Immediately after the cavity flush
e: Rectal temperature is always taken LAST in the sexual abuse examination protocol. The rectal thermometer inserted before rectal swabs and flush could destroy or contaminate the rectal evidence — displacing semen, breaking spermatozoa, and introducing lubricant contamination. Document in the record that temperature was obtained last in order to preserve rectal evidence integrity.

q: When collecting DNA swabs from the vaginal orifice of a dog suspected of sexual abuse, the ASPCA protocol specifies:
o: One swab per area, fixed in 10% formalin for histopathology
Three swabs per area, immediately frozen at −20°C (−4°F) in a sealed plastic container
One swab per area, placed immediately in a sealed plastic tube with transport medium
A minimum of two swabs per area, air-dried, and stored in paper envelopes with chain-of-custody labelling
e: The ASPCA protocol specifies a minimum of two swabs per area, to allow duplicate analysis (one for immediate testing, one held in reserve). Swabs must be air-dried before packaging — wet swabs in sealed containers degrade DNA rapidly. Store in paper (never plastic). Label with case number, exact anatomical location, date, time, and collector's name. Formalin destroys DNA; frozen plastic containers also degrade samples through condensation.

q: Samples collected by flushing the vaginal cavity should be stored in which container and at which temperature?
o: 10% buffered formalin container, room temperature
Red-top tube (no additives), refrigerated at 4°C (39.2°F)
Purple-top EDTA tube, frozen at −20°C (−4°F)
Green-top lithium heparin tube, room temperature
e: The cavity flush (vaginal or rectal) is collected in a sterile red-top tube (no additives, no anticoagulant) and stored refrigerated at 4°C (39.2°F) — not frozen. Freezing disrupts cellular morphology needed for cytology (sperm identification) and can degrade some DNA. EDTA and heparin anticoagulants can interfere with downstream PCR-based DNA analysis. Formalin destroys both DNA and cellular morphology.

q: Which of the following is a PENETRATION injury finding in a sexual abuse case, as opposed to a restraint injury?
o: Ligature marks around the muzzle
Bilateral flank bruising from grip marks
Lacerations of the vulvar lips with weak vaginal introitus tone
Abrasions on the dorsal neck from head restraint
e: Penetration injuries include: bruising and tearing of genital/rectal tissue, vaginal or anal dilation with weak sphincter tone, bleeding, prolapse, perforation, and retained foreign objects. Ligature marks around the muzzle, bilateral flank bruising, and dorsal neck abrasions are all restraint injuries — caused by holding or immobilising the animal during the assault, not by the sexual act itself. Distinguishing these two categories helps reconstruct the event.

q: Spermatozoa identified on urinalysis sediment examination of a female dog is MOST significant because:
o: It confirms that the dog was recently used for breeding without owner consent
Spermatozoa are a normal urinalysis finding in intact female dogs in oestrus
It indicates the dog mated naturally, which is not a cruelty concern
Sperm reaching the bladder via the short female urethra following vaginal assault is a specific forensic finding supporting sexual abuse
e: Spermatozoa in the urine of a female dog is abnormal and forensically significant. The female dog's short, straight urethra allows semen deposited in the vagina to migrate into the bladder. This finding on routine UA sediment is a high-yield exam point — it is specifically mentioned in the ASPCA protocol as a reason to perform urinalysis in all suspected sexual abuse cases. Spermatozoa are not a normal UA finding.

q: The ASPCA sexual abuse protocol requires a follow-up examination at 24–48 hours primarily because:
o: The follow-up is required to administer prophylactic antibiotics
Injuries including bruising and mucosal tears may not be visible at initial presentation and evolve over the following 24–48 hours
A second examiner must verify all findings from the initial examination for legal purposes
DNA evidence degrades after 24 hours and must be recollected
e: Soft tissue injuries — particularly bruising and mucosal tears from penetration — may not be visible at initial examination and become apparent over the following 24–48 hours as haemorrhage and inflammatory changes develop. The follow-up exam is a required component of the ASPCA protocol and should be planned at the initial visit. Document all new or evolving findings with photographs at the follow-up.

q: Which forensic light source parameter is specified in the ASPCA sexual abuse protocol for surface examination?
o: 415 nm excitation filter (or Wood's lamp UV) combined with orange-tinted goggles to filter background and visualise fluorescent material
Standard white-light examination under a magnifying glass
Polarised light at 550 nm for skin surface examination
Infrared light at 900 nm with a clear filter
e: The ASPCA protocol specifies a 415 nm excitation filter (forensic light source) with orange goggles, OR a standard Wood's lamp (long-wave UV ~365 nm). The orange goggles are essential — they filter the background blue excitation light and allow biological fluorescence to be visualised. Without the goggles, fluorescent areas are obscured by the excitation light. Areas of fluorescence are documented by photograph before any swabbing.
